steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on scale-free algorithms for adversarial reinforcement learning, i.e. algorithms that don't need to know the scale of the losses. Motivate the problem, explain what goes wrong with existing scale-free bandit methods, and list our contributions (SCB, SCB-IX, SCB-RL).

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. RL and adversarial MDPs; the bounded-loss assumption and why it breaks
2. Scale-free algorithms: prior work in online learning and bandits, and its problems
3. Our approach: the SCB framework
4. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Setting and motivation
- RL: agent interacts with unknown environment, improve policy, minimize cumulative loss through time
- environment = MDP with unknown transition function; focus: adversarial MDP (losses generated adversarially)
- virtually all prior RL work: rewards/losses uniformly bounded, e.g. mean reward per state-action pair within [0, 1]
- condition needed to set hyper-parameters (learning rate) properly -> low regret
- real world: no natural bound, e.g. quantitative trading (stock prices vary over time and across stocks); scale often unknown a priori -> most existing algorithms fail

2. Scale-free algorithms
- we initiate study of scale-free RL in MDPs: no prior knowledge on scale of losses
- studied in online learning literature; for decision-making under uncertainty only Multi-armed Bandits (MAB) = 1 -layer MDP, single state
- existing scale-free MAB = online learning algorithms adapted to bandit feedback -> fundamental problems:
  - limitations of regularizers: no scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm minimax optimal (optimal to logarithm terms)
  - only bound regret of important weighted estimators -> expected regret only, no high probability regret
  - dependence on important weighted estimators -> no generalization to adversarial MDP with unknown transitions

3. SCB
- first scale-free algorithm for adversarial MDPs with unknown transition function
- unified framework: Scale Clipping Bound (SCB); applies to MAB and MDP; improves previous results across the board
- Table 1: comparison with prior works

4. Contributions
- SCB: scale-free adversarial MAB, minimax optimal expected regret, no knowledge of loss magnitude; removes \log(n), \log(T) factors; matches minimax lower-bound up to constant factors; answers an open problem positively
- SCB-IX: built on SCB; first scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm with high probability regret bound
- SCB-RL: adversarial MDPs; first scale-free algorithm with \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) high probability regret bound; unknown transition, unbounded losses, bandit feedback

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is the problem where an agent interacts with an unknown environment and tries to improve its policy and minimize its cumulative loss over time. Usually the environment is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) where the transition function is unknown. In this paper we focus on the adversarial MDP setting, in which the losses can be generated adversarially. It is curious that almost all prior works on RL assume that the rewards/losses are uniformly bounded, for example that the mean reward for any state-action pair is within [0, 1]. This regularity condition is very important, because it is what lets existing algorithms set their hyper-parameters such as the learning rate properly so that they get low regrets. But in many real-world applications there is no natural loss bound like this. For example, in quantitative trading, stock prices can vary a lot over time and also across different stocks. And more importantly, the algorithm often does not know the scale of this variance a priori. In settings like these most existing algorithms don't work anymore.

Because of these limitations, in this paper we start the study of scale-free RL algorithms in MDPs, which means algorithms that do not need any prior knowledge on the scale of the losses. Scale-free algorithms have been studied before in the online learning literature. But for decision-making under uncertainty, the only relevant studies are about Multi-armed Bandits (MAB), which can be seen as a 1 -layer MDP with only one state. The existing algorithms for scale-free MAB basically take algorithms designed for online learning and adapt them to the bandit feedback setting. This causes some fundamental problems. First, because of the limitations of regularizers, none of the existing scale-free adversarial MAB algorithms can achieve minimax optimality (i.e., optimal to logarithm terms). Second, existing works only bound the regret that comes from the important weighted estimators, so they can only bound the expected regret, and this cannot be generalized to high probability regret. Third, since the existing algorithms depend on important weighted estimators, their results cannot be generalized to the setting of adversarial MDP with unknown transition function.

3. SCB
- first scale-free algorithm for adversarial MDPs with unknown transition function
- unified framework: Scale Clipping Bound (SCB); applies to MAB and MDP; improves previous results across the board
- Table 1: comparison with prior works

4. Contributions
- SCB: scale-free adversarial MAB, minimax optimal expected regret, no knowledge of loss magnitude; removes \log(n), \log(T) factors; matches minimax lower-bound up to constant factors; answers an open problem positively
- SCB-IX: built on SCB; first scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm with high probability regret bound
- SCB-RL: adversarial MDPs; first scale-free algorithm with \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) high probability regret bound; unknown transition, unbounded losses, bandit feedback

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is the problem where an agent interacts with an unknown environment and tries to improve its policy and minimize its cumulative loss over time. Usually the environment is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) where the transition function is unknown. In this paper we focus on the adversarial MDP setting, in which the losses can be generated adversarially. It is curious that almost all prior works on RL assume that the rewards/losses are uniformly bounded, for example that the mean reward for any state-action pair is within [0, 1]. This regularity condition is very important, because it is what lets existing algorithms set their hyper-parameters such as the learning rate properly so that they get low regrets. But in many real-world applications there is no natural loss bound like this. For example, in quantitative trading, stock prices can vary a lot over time and also across different stocks. And more importantly, the algorithm often does not know the scale of this variance a priori. In settings like these most existing algorithms don't work anymore.

Because of these limitations, in this paper we start the study of scale-free RL algorithms in MDPs, which means algorithms that do not need any prior knowledge on the scale of the losses. Scale-free algorithms have been studied before in the online learning literature. But for decision-making under uncertainty, the only relevant studies are about Multi-armed Bandits (MAB), which can be seen as a 1 -layer MDP with only one state. The existing algorithms for scale-free MAB basically take algorithms designed for online learning and adapt them to the bandit feedback setting. This causes some fundamental problems. First, because of the limitations of regularizers, none of the existing scale-free adversarial MAB algorithms can achieve minimax optimality (i.e., optimal to logarithm terms). Second, existing works only bound the regret that comes from the important weighted estimators, so they can only bound the expected regret, and this cannot be generalized to high probability regret. Third, since the existing algorithms depend on important weighted estimators, their results cannot be generalized to the setting of adversarial MDP with unknown transition function.

In this paper we propose the first scale-free algorithm for adversarial MDPs with unknown transition function. We design a unified framework that we call Scale Clipping Bound (SCB). The framework can be used for both MAB and MDP, and it improves the previous results a lot across the board. Our technical contributions are summarized below, and Table 1 gives an overview that compares our results with the ones in prior works.

- 1. We propose SCB, which is a scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm that gets minimax optimal expected regret bounds without knowing the loss magnitude. Our result gets rid of the \log(n) and \log(T) factors that prior works have, and it matches the minimax lower-bound up to constant factors. This answers positively the open problem that was raised in prior work.

- 2. Based on the idea of SCB we build SCB-IX, which is the first scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm that gets a high probability regret bound.

- 3. Finally, we extend these ideas to the setting of adversarial MDPs and present SCB-RL. It is the first scale-free algorithm that achieves a \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) high probability regret bound for adversarial MDP with unknown transition function, unbounded losses and bandit feedback.

steps.name: cited_draft
steps.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is the problem where an agent interacts with an unknown environment and tries to improve its policy and minimize its cumulative loss over time. Usually the environment is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) where the transition function is unknown. In this paper we focus on the adversarial MDP setting, in which the losses can be generated adversarially [1]. It is curious that almost all prior works on RL assume that the rewards/losses are uniformly bounded, for example that the mean reward for any state-action pair is within [0,1]. This regularity condition is very important, because it is what lets existing algorithms set their hyper-parameters such as the learning rate properly so that they get low regrets. But in many real-world applications there is no natural loss bound like this. For example, in quantitative trading, stock prices can vary a lot over time and also across different stocks. And more importantly, the algorithm often does not know the scale of this variance a priori. In settings like these most existing algorithms don't work anymore.

Because of these limitations, in this paper we start the study of scale-free RL algorithms in MDPs, which means algorithms that do not need any prior knowledge on the scale of the losses. Scale-free algorithms have been studied before in the online learning literature [2,3,4,5,6,7]. But for decision-making under uncertainty, the only relevant studies are about Multi-armed Bandits (MAB) [8,9,10,11], which can be seen as a 1 -layer MDP with only one state. The existing algorithms for scale-free MAB basically take algorithms designed for online learning and adapt them to the bandit feedback setting. This causes some fundamental problems. First, because of the limitations of regularizers, none of the existing scale-free adversarial MAB algorithms can achieve minimax optimality (i.e., optimal to logarithm terms). Second, existing works only bound the regret that comes from the important weighted estimators, so they can only bound the expected regret, and this cannot be generalized to high probability regret. Third, since the existing algorithms depend on important weighted estimators, their results cannot be generalized to the setting of adversarial MDP with unknown transition function.

In this paper we propose the first scale-free algorithm for adversarial MDPs with unknown transition function. We design a unified framework that we call Scale Clipping Bound (SCB). The framework can be used for both MAB and MDP, and it improves the previous results a lot across the board. Our technical contributions are summarized below, and Table 1 gives an overview that compares our results with the ones in prior works.

- 1. We propose SCB, which is a scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm that gets minimax optimal expected regret bounds without knowing the loss magnitude. Our result gets rid of the \log(n) and \log(T) factors that prior works have, and it matches the minimax lower-bound [15] up to constant factors. This answers positively the open problem that was raised in [8].

- 2. Based on the idea of SCB we build SCB-IX, which is the first scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm that gets a high probability regret bound.

- 3. Finally, we extend these ideas to the setting of adversarial MDPs and present SCB-RL. It is the first scale-free algorithm that achieves a \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) high probability regret bound for adversarial MDP with unknown transition function, unbounded losses and bandit feedback.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) refers to the problem of an agent interacting with an unknown environment with the goal of improving its policy and minimizing cumulative loss through time. The environment is commonly modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) with an unknown transition function. In this paper we focus on the adversarial MDP setting, where the losses may be generated adversarially [1]. Curiously, virtually all prior works on RL assume that the rewards/losses are uniformly bounded, e.g. that the mean reward for any state-action pair is within [0,1]. This regularity condition is crucial in allowing existing algorithms to properly set hyper-parameters such as the learning rate to achieve low regrets. In many real-world applications, however, such a natural loss bound does not always exist. For instance, in quantitative trading, stock prices can vary significantly over time and across different stocks. More importantly, the scale of such variance is often not known to the algorithm a priori. In such settings, most existing algorithms no longer work.

Motivated by these limitations, in this paper we initiate the study of scale-free RL algorithms in MDPs, i.e. algorithms that require no prior knowledge on the scale of the losses. Scale-free algorithms have previously been studied in the online learning literature [2,3,4,5,6,7]. However, for decision-making under uncertainty, the only relevant studies are limited to Multi-armed Bandits (MAB) [8,9,10,11], which can be considered as a 1 -layer MDP with a single state. Existing algorithms for scale-free MAB essentially adapt algorithms designed for online learning to the bandit feedback setting, which leads to some fundamental problems. First, due to the limitations of regularizers, no existing scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm can achieve minimax optimality (i.e., optimal to logarithm terms). Secondly, existing works only bound the regret incurred by the important weighted estimators; as a result, they can only bound the expected regret and cannot be generalized to high probability regret. Third, given the existing algorithms' dependence on important weighted estimators, their results cannot be generalized to the setting of adversarial MDP with unknown transition function.

In this paper, we propose the first scale-free algorithm for adversarial MDPs with unknown transition function. We design a unified framework called Scale Clipping Bound (SCB), which can be applied to both MAB and MDP and significantly improves previous results across the board. Our technical contributions are summarized below, and an overview comparing our results with those in prior works can be found in Table 1.

- 1. We propose SCB, a scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm that achieves minimax optimal expected regret bounds without knowledge of the loss magnitude. Our result eliminates the \log(n) and \log(T) factors in prior works and matches the minimax lower-bound [15] up to constant factors. This gives a positive answer to the open problem raised in [8].

- 2. Based on the idea of SCB, we build SCB-IX, the first scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm achieving a high probability regret bound.

- 3. Finally, we extend the above ideas to the setting of adversarial MDPs and present SCB-RL, the first scale-free algorithm that achieves a \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) high probability regret bound for adversarial MDP with unknown transition function, unbounded losses and bandit feedback.
